catalog_quote: It appears probable that neither the accent nor vowel length are phonemic in Southern Ŋarigu. Both a tonic stress accent and a secondary accent could be distinguished. The tonic stress accent was associated with a very slight rise in pitch and usually fell on the first syllable of a word. There was however a group of words of three or more syllables in which the main stress fell on the second syllable, and a secondary stress frequently fell on the final syllable of three-syllable words. They are: budalag ... goanna ... wirgara ... whereabouts? The second syllable, which bears the accent in these words, begins with d, r, l, m or n, (except in the last example) ... it is not possible to tell to what extent the accent is conditioned by the environment: there are some words with similar sound-groups where the accent falls on the initial syllable, e.g. mirigan ... dog, dununalug ... to stare…

new_statements.quote: It appears probable that neither the accent nor vowel length are phonemic in Southern Ngarigu. Both a tonic stress accent and a secondary accent could be distinguished. The tonic stress accent was associated with a very slight rise in pitch and usually fell on the first syllable of a word. There was however a group of words of three or more syllables in which the main stress fell on the second syllable, and a secondary stress frequently fell on the final syllable of three-syllable words. ... The only possible conclusion from our limited material is that the main accent is usually initial, and that certain consonants are associated with the accent on the second syllable in words of three or more syllables.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Main (tonic) stress normally falls on the first syllable of the word; in a lexically listed set of about 16 words of three or more syllables (whose second syllable begins with d, r, l, m or n) main stress falls instead on the second syllable, possibly conditioned by consonant environment and third-syllable vowel length; stress is not contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'A weaker secondary accent usually fell on the last syllable if the vowel was long or half-long: balan ['ba,la:n] woman.. In words of four syllables the secondary accent fell on the third syllable if that contained a long vowel: gambawali to cry.' In the second-syllable-stress words a secondary stress frequently falls on the final syllable of trisyllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Listed words with second-syllable main stress (p.172): budalag goanna, budira clever man, djarimiŋ flash, djiralgal lizard, yaraman horse, miribi thunder, murili bad woman, njarala to listen, djamalaŋ platypus, djimaŋgal thrush, dinabili dirty, guniriŋ silly, gunamudanj poisoner, yalagan good, waligaḍa legendary little people, wirgara whereabouts; counter-examples with similar sound-groups but initial stress (mirigan dog, dununalug to stare). Authors note the rule may be 'very complex' and material is scanty.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, from elicited citation forms remembered by dispersed Southern Ngarigu (Delegate / Snowy River) rememberers recorded in the 1960s; speakers no longer used the grammar. Koch 2016 (sec. 4.3) restates the same finding and calls H&M the only phonological source for Ngarigu.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes 'Southern Ngarigu', the variety of Ngarigu remembered by people originally from Delegate and the upper Snowy River (NSW/Victoria border), recorded by Hercus in the 1960s from rememberers who no longer used the grammar. Glottolog 5.1 files Ngarigu (AUSTLANG S46; retired ISO xni) together with Jaitmathang/Omeo (retired ISO xjt), Walgalu and Nyamudy under sout2770 'Southern Inland Yuin' with no dialect children; Koch 2016 treats all of these as varieties of one Ngarigu language and names Hercus & Mathews as its only phonological description. our earlier survey classification (no source found, 'Hercus 1969 survey = wordlist only') was wrong: the survey contains a phonology with an explicit accentuation section.

sources.quote: It appears probable that neither the accent nor vowel length are phonemic in Southern Ngarigu. Both a tonic stress accent and a secondary accent could be distinguished. sources.note: Accent and vowel length probably not phonemic; tonic stress accent (slight pitch rise) usually on the first syllable; a listed group of ~16 words of 3+ syllables has main stress on the 2nd syllable (2nd syllable begins with d, r, l, m or n); weaker secondary accent usually on the last syllable if its vowel is long/half-long, or on the 3rd syllable of 4-syllable words if long; vocabulary entries carry stress-marked phonetic transcriptions.

sources.note: Restates Hercus & Mathews: 'while stress is normally on the first syllable, there are at least 16 words where it is the second of three syllables that receives the accent'; no clear rule, but six examples have rr as second consonant; unstressed-vowel reduction toward schwa (attributed to English influence). States H&M (1969, 1986) is the only source that explicitly discusses Ngarigu phonetics/phonology.
